Q: How would you save a simple settings/configuration file in Python? A:

config.json

{
  "mongo": "mongodb://test:test@127.0.0.1:27017/?retryWrites=true",
  "mssql": "mssql+pymssql://test:test/?@127.0.01.1:1433/SomeMSSQLDb",
  "postgresql": "dbname=pgdb host=postgres port=5432 user=test password=test"
}

Python code:

import json
from pathlib import Path

CONFIG_FILE = Path(__file__).parent / 'config.json'

def load_config():
    with open(CONFIG_FILE) as f:
        return json.load(f)

config = load_config()
MONGO_URI = config['mongo']
MSSQL_URI = config['mssql']
POSTGRESQL_URI = config['postgresql']

Q: Does Scandit Data Capture SDK support barcode scanning from images in Android UI tests? A:

  1. Does the Scandit SDK support decoding barcode images during Android instrumentation/UI tests?

    Yes. The Scandit Data Capture SDK supports decoding from static images via BitmapFrameSource, which works in instrumentation tests. It uses the same DataCaptureContext and barcode capture setup as the camera path, so no special test mode is required.

  2. Is BitmapFrameSource the recommended approach?

    Yes. BitmapFrameSource is intended for scanning from static images instead of the camera. From the Scandit documentation:

    • Use BitmapFrameSource.of(bitmap) with an ARGB_8888 bitmap.

    • Set it as the frame source on DataCaptureContext and call switchToDesiredState(FrameSourceState.ON).

    • It emits one frame and then turns off automatically.

    Your production code already follows this pattern when bitmap != null, so it is the right path for tests.

  3. Limitations when running on an emulator during UI tests

    • Camera path: Emulators have limited camera support, which can cause issues when using the camera.

    • BitmapFrameSource path: This path does not use the camera, so emulator camera limitations do not apply. Using BitmapFrameSource is a good way to run barcode tests on emulators.

  4. Constraint: you cannot modify production code

    The main challenge is how the app receives the bitmap. The test must trigger the same path the app uses in production (e.g. intent extras, URI, file path).

If the app accepts a bitmap via intent extras (we can do):

// In your UI test
val bitmap = BitmapFactory.decodeResource(
    InstrumentationRegistry.getInstrumentation().targetContext.resources,
    R.drawable.test_barcode
)
val intent = Intent(ApplicationProvider.getApplicationContext(), YourScannerActivity::class.java)
intent.putExtra("bitmap", bitmap)  // or your app's extra key

ActivityScenario.launch(intent)

If the app loads from a URI or file path:

  • Put a test barcode image in the app’s assets or files directory.

  • Launch the activity with an intent that includes the URI or path the app expects.

Q: Ktor TCP readbyte A:

Do I need to create some proprietary wrapper which will split the payload and will contain the TVL structure of the data payload and customize read function in ktor accordingly?

TCP does not have packet boundaries, it's a continuous stream. So creating your own packet structure with a length prefix is very common in TCP-based protocols, and is probably the most reliable approach.

Or is there some other option I mean is there some function in the ktor which will buffer all bytes from one tcp packet first and than it will return me that data instantly without waiting for some ending character or proprietary length field?

Again, TCP doesn't really have packets as such. The receiver can't really tell the difference between one 5000-byte write and five 1000-byte writes. It therefore cannot know for sure that it is "done" receiving data. Almost all protocols use either a length field or a delimiter.

On the Internet, a typical MTU (maximum IP packet size) is 1500, so if you write 5000 bytes it will always be split into some number of TCP segments (typical Internet MTU is 1500 so a typical max TCP segment size is around 1440 bytes), delivered within 4–5 separate IP packets, and the receiver will reassemble them back into a continuous stream of bytes.

So if the receiver requests "recv(9001)" then it will indeed receive the 5000 bytes that are currently buffered, but it does not have a guarantee that it's the whole thing.

And also if I will send packet using the TCP ip and the length will be let's say over the 5000 bytes.

Will it arrive in that size cuz in some devices there probably might be the internal buffer size limited or not?

TCP has flow control (the "sliding window" system), where the sender is only allowed to send a certain amount of bytes at once, and the receiver incrementally extends that window as it processes the received data. The extra data is therefore never lost, but held by the sender.

So if the receiver really is incapable of handling e.g. more than 1k at once, then it will indicate that in its "window size". Your 5000 bytes will be stored in the sender's buffer first, and will be gradually delivered whenever the receiver ACKs what it has processed.

The same happens if the receiver simply doesn't call "read()" or "recv()" – its OS will buffer a certain amount of received data, then it stops extending the window, and the sender understands that it's not allowed to send more.

Also do I need to include additional verification into that packet or can I relay on data layer packet verification?

As far as data corruption goes, you can mostly rely on the lower layers being reliable. Many application protocols exist without any error checking of their own.

However, you should be using TLS these days – and TLS has inherent verification, as the same MAC that prevents tampering with packets also detects any other corruption (should it manage to sneak by the checksums in TCP and all the lower layers).

And also the time and the latency I probably cannot relay on time when we are talking receiving data using TCP over long distances so waiting fixed amount of time after each data byte in receiving function won't be probably reliable or?

It's unnecessary. TCP already handles flow control and congestion control for you, and the OS handles buffering of received data.
